query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored post-forging annealing treatment in the range of 550–650°C will relax interfacial stresses and promote the formation of coherent nanometer‐scale precipitates along the dual-phase lamellar colony boundaries, thereby mitigating dislocation pile-ups, reducing local stress concentrations, and overcoming limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or enhancing strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure consisting of dual-phase lamellar colonies produced by conventional processing, exhibiting dislocation pile-ups at internal lamellar boundaries that lead to local stress concentrations and brittle failure under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.intervention: A single, tailored post-forging annealing treatment performed at 550–650°C for an optimized duration to allow interfacial stress relaxation and to trigger the controlled formation of coherent nano-precipitates along the lamellar interfaces.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation under standard ambient testing conditions typical for structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent, nanometer-scale precipitates that form at the lamellar boundaries during the annealing process.
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment relaxes residual stresses at the internal lamellar interfaces and induces the formation of finely dispersed nano-precipitates that act to facilitate dislocation transmission across boundaries. This suppresses the accumulation of dislocations (pile-ups), thereby reducing local stress concentrations that lead to microcracking and brittle fracture, while the precipitates themselves contribute to strengthening through precipitation hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to exhibit improved tensile ductility (increased strain to failure) and maintained or enhanced tensile strength relative to the untreated material by alleviating the concentration of dislocations and associated local stress and damage.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic HEA shows limited room-temperature ductility and brittleness due to dislocation pile-up at lamellar interfaces, which creates local stress spikes and microcrack initiation during tensile deformation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to eutectic HEAs with dual-phase lamellar microstructures under room-temperature tensile conditions. Its effectiveness may not extend to alloys with significantly different microstructural features or operating conditions beyond ambient temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise annealing duration required for optimal nano-precipitate formation, the uniformity of precipitate distribution along all interfaces, and the balance between precipitate-induced strengthening and potential embrittlement remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of eutectic HEA samples with the described dual-phase lamellar microstructure. Subject one group to the tailored post-forging annealing treatment at 550–650°C for varying durations, while keeping a control group in the as-processed state. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess the formation and distribution of nano-precipitates along lamellar boundaries. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests to measure ductility (strain to failure) and tensile strength.
measurements: TEM analysis for nano-precipitate presence, size, and distribution at lamellar interfaces
Room-temperature tensile stress–strain curves to determine yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility (elongation to failure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not display a significant formation of coherent nano-precipitates at the lamellar boundaries, or if tensile testing shows no improvement (or a degradation) in ductility and strength relative to the control group, then the hypothesis that the annealing treatment overcomes the dislocation pile-up-related brittleness is falsified.

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. chosen.conditions: Annealing at 550–650°C following a forging step, with subsequent evaluation via room-temperature tensile tests and in-situ TEM to verify reduced dislocation pile-ups
chosen.why: This intervention most directly targets the unexplained behavior of stress-concentrating dislocation pile-ups at the phase boundaries. By tailoring the annealing parameters to relax and slightly modify the boundary structure, the treatment is expected to facilitate smoother dislocation transmission, thereby reducing local stress concentrations and microcrack initiation, all while retaining or improving the alloy’s strength. This approach uses standard thermomechanical processing techniques widely accepted in the field.

decision.trend: Early work on eutectic HEAs—as exemplified by the 2014 study (PMC4145285) on an AlCoCrFeNi alloy with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure—focused on casting followed by cold working and standard heat treatments. These methods increased strength and even improved some ductility by refining lamellar spacing, yet they did not resolve the problem of localized dislocation pile‐up at the lamellar interfaces. Subsequent studies using conventional thermomechanical processes further enhanced strength but left the intrinsic issue of concentrated stress sites at internal boundaries largely unmitigated.
decision.unsolved: The critical unsolved challenge is how to relieve dislocation pile-ups at the dual-phase lamellar colony interfaces that lead to local stress concentrations, microcracking, and brittle failure under room-temperature tensile loading, all while preserving or even boosting overall strength.
decision.lever: a tailored post-forging annealing treatment (e.g., at 550–650°C) designed to relax interfacial stresses and trigger nano‐precipitate formation at the lamellar boundaries
decision.why: This intervention directly targets the dislocation pile-up issue by engineering the internal boundaries: the annealing step promotes boundary relaxation and the controlled emergence of coherent, nanometer-scale precipitates that facilitate dislocation transmission across the lamellae. This approach is a logical extension of prior thermomechanical processing trends and precisely addresses the niche concern of mitigating local stress concentrations while retaining or enhancing strength under room-temperature conditions.
